claims.claim: Asked why he is drawn to deceptions that turn out to be true, Wolfe says it must be the unconscious hope that some of his will.
claims.quote: the unconscious hope that some of mine will

claims.claim: Scenes Horn could not have witnessed are sourced within the fiction (an unnamed kite builder; prayers written by Horn and Nettle who heard Silk pray), and Wolfe points to a page in Exodus.

claims.feature: happened / probably happened / must have happened
claims.claim: Horn and Nettle tell what happened, what probably happened and what must have happened, in dramatic form; their account is necessarily subjective and they make mistakes.
claims.quote: what probably happened, and what must have happened

claims.claim: Wolfe concedes the Mint/Marble location swap in Exodus is his mistake; Langford notes readers had been reading subtleties into his least typos.

claims.feature: literal answer to a symbolic question
claims.claim: Asked who or what Oreb is, Wolfe answers only that Oreb is a night chough, declining the symbolic reading the questioner wanted.

claims.feature: answers deferred to the next book
claims.claim: Some questions (Quetzal's motive) are answered only by telling the reader to read the next series, keeping the withholding in force.
claims.quote: You will have to read The Book

claims.claim: Wolfe reads Tolkien as having uncovered a forgotten Folk Law and built Middle-earth as a means of displaying it in the clearest light, planting the truth that society need not be as we see it.
claims.source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
claims.quote: society need not be as we see it around us

claims.claim: He describes rationing The Fellowship to one chapter an evening while permitting himself to reread earlier chapters endlessly, the habit of the rereader he later writes for.
claims.source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
claims.quote: no more than a single chapter each evening

claims.feature: etymology inside and outside the story
claims.claim: Tolkien's reply to Wolfe's fan letter distinguishes a word's etymology within the story from the author's source for it, a distinction Wolfe's own Latinate diction depends on.
claims.source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)

claims.feature: trust the text / do not trust the text
claims.claim: Gaiman's first two rules: trust the text implicitly because the answers are in there, and do not trust it farther than you can throw it because it may go off in your hand.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.

claims.claim: The books subtly reshape themselves while you are away; Peace was a gentle Midwestern memoir on first reading and a horror novel on the second or third.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: It only became a horror novel on the second

claims.claim: Wolfe is the kind of clever writer who sees no need to point out his cleverness; the intelligence serves the tale and makes the reader smart too.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: He is smart to make you smart as well.

claims.claim: Rule 8 asserts the author was there and knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror, i.e. the withheld fact is known and recoverable.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: He knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror

claims.claim: Gaiman reports Wolfe solving a ninety-year-old murder from a press clipping (the matches by the railway tracks), evidence of the engineer's mind behind the clue-planting.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe / journal

claims.feature: story knows more than it says
claims.claim: Clute's summary law: a Wolfe story always knows more than it says and can almost never be fully grasped on a first reading.
claims.quote: A Wolfe story always knows more than it says

verdicts.trueWording: I'm sure it must be the unconscious hope that some of mine will.
verdicts.note: Q2 on the page: 'What is his [Wolfe's] attraction to [pretences or deceptions that turn out to be true]? - I'm sure it must be the unconscious hope that some of mine will.' Quote matches word for word; both limbs (the question asked, the answer given) are on the page. The bracketed restorations of the abbreviated question are the editor's, as the page states up front.

Q21 asks about scenes 'hard to imagine Horn hearing about from witnesses'. Wolfe: 'Horn's information on the first came from the kite builder, who asked that his name not be used. Silk's prayers (etc.) were written by Horn and Nettle, who had heard him pray many times. Please reread Exodus, p. 371.' Every limb - unnamed kite builder, prayers written by Horn and Nettle who heard Silk pray, the Exodus page pointer - is present.

verdicts.trueWording: Horn and Nettle are doing their best to tell you what happened, what probably happened, and what must have happened, in dramatic form.
verdicts.note: Q21a ('How trustworthy a narrator is Horn?'). The page continues: 'They are human beings, however, and make mistakes. (We all do, especially me.) Their account is subjective, necessarily, as all accounts are.' Quote exact; the subjectivity and mistake limbs both present.

verdicts.trueWording: You're right, and they are my mistakes.
verdicts.note: Q28 asks about Mint and Marble seeming to exchange places near the end of Exodus, deliberate or an auctorial/editorial mistake. Quote exact. The editorial aside is signed with initials - '[DRL: You can't imagine how relieved this made me! We read subtleties into Wolfe's least typos....]' - and the name Langford does not appear on cc77 itself; the publication's own index at ansible.uk/cc/ states 'Cloud Chamber is another bloody Langford fanzine', so the attribution holds within the source.

Q1: 'Who or what is Oreb? - Oreb is a night chough.' Quote exact, and the declining-the-symbolic-reading limb is carried by the editorial bracket that follows: 'Needless to say, the questioner hoped for an answer concerning the bird's symbolism or significance....'

verdicts.trueWording: You will have to read The Book of the Short Sun.
verdicts.note: Q23: 'What was Quetzal's motive in wanting a thriving human colony on Green? - You will have to read The Book of the Short Sun.' The quote fragment is verbatim. That Short Sun is the next series is confirmed lower on the same page: 'It is leading to the Book of the Short Sun. It will deal with the colonists...'

verdicts.trueWording: What he did, then, was to plant in my consciousness and yours the truth that society need not be as we see it around us.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Supporting limbs on the page: 'There he found a quality -- let us call it Folk Law -- that has almost disappeared from his world and ours'; 'He uncovered a forgotten wisdom among the barbarian tribes... he had not only uncovered but understood it'; 'Having learned that, he created in Middle-earth a means of displaying it in the clearest and most favourable possible light.' The page's wording is 'created in Middle-earth a means' where the claim says 'built Middle-earth as a means'; the import is the same.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that this rationing is 'the habit of the rereader he later writes for' - the essay says nothing about Wolfe's own writing, his readers, or rereading his own books
verdicts.trueWording: forcing myself to read no more than a single chapter each evening
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and the rationing limbs are fully supported: the book is The Fellowship of the Ring, and 'The catch, my out, the stratagem by which I escaped the bonds of my own law, was that I could read that chapter as many times as I wished; and that I could also return to the chapter I had read the night before... There were evenings on which I reread the entire book up the point -- The Council of Elrond, let us say -- at which I had forced myself to stop.' Only the closing gloss tying the habit to his own later authorship is absent from the page.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that this is 'a distinction Wolfe's own Latinate diction depends on' - the essay never discusses Wolfe's diction or vocabulary
verdicts.trueWording: The etymology of words and names in my story has two sides.
verdicts.note: The Tolkien letter is reproduced in full on the page, dated 7th November 1966 and addressed 'Dear Mr Wolfe', after Wolfe writes 'ten years later I wrote J. R. R. Tolkien a fan letter. He answered it'. The distinction limb is exact: '(1) their etymology within the story; and (2) the sources from which I, as an author, derive them.' 'two sides' appears word for word. Only the trailing claim about Wolfe's own diction is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: 1) Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.
verdicts.note: Rule 1 exact. Rule 2 on the page: 'Do not trust the text farther than you can throw it, if that far. It's tricksy and desperate stuff, and it may go off in your hand at any time.' Both limbs of the claim are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: It only became a horror novel on the second or the third reading.
verdicts.note: Rule 3 in full: 'Reread... And anyway, the books will subtly reshape themselves while you are away from them. Peace really was a gentle Midwestern memoir the first time I read it. It only became a horror novel on the second or the third reading.' Quote verbatim; both limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: He is smart to make you smart as well.
verdicts.note: Rule 7: 'There are two kinds of clever writer. The ones that point out how clever they are, and the ones who see no need to point out how clever they are. Gene Wolfe is of the second kind, and the intelligence is less important than the tale. He is not smart to make you feel stupid. He is smart to make you smart as well.' Quote exact. The claim's 'the intelligence serves the tale' renders the page's 'the intelligence is less important than the tale'.

verdicts.trueWording: He was there. He saw it happen. He knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror that night.
verdicts.note: Rule 8 exact, quote verbatim as a prefix. The 'known' limb is rule 8 itself; the 'recoverable' limb is not in rule 8 but is supported elsewhere on the same page by rule 1, 'Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.'

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the anecdote is 'evidence of the engineer's mind behind the clue-planting' - the post never connects it to clue-planting or any technique in Wolfe's fiction (the clues in the anecdote are the police's, in a real murder case)
verdicts.trueWording: He has an engineer's mind that takes things apart to see how they work and then puts them back together.
verdicts.note: Fetched the journal URL itself (HTTP 200, live host). Quote verbatim, and every factual limb is on the page: 'I once read him an account of a baffling murder, committed ninety years ago... proceeded off-handedly to offer a simple and likely explanation', plus the closing parenthesis '(It was the matches on the ground, by the railway tracks, that Gene pointed to, in the old press clipping murder case, that cracked it; but of course by then the tramp was ninety years dead...)'. The post also identifies these as the first two paragraphs of the How to Read Gene Wolfe essay. Only the clue-planting gloss is the researcher's inference.

verdicts.trueWording: A Wolfe story always knows more than it says, and can almost never be fully grasped on a first-time reading.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. The entry is signed '[JC]' - John Clute - and the site footer reads 'Site and SFE content (c) 2011-2026 John Clute & David Langford', so the Clute attribution is supported on the page. The claim writes 'first reading' where the page has 'first-time reading'; the quoted limb itself is untouched by that.
